A Blog post by Amazon on Hugging Face
A Blog post by Amazon on Hugging Face
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up enti

en.reason: Second-order HOPE expert pruning targets Qwen3.5-122B's 48 MoE layers of 256 experts, where expert MLPs occupy 95% of ~250 GB memory though each token uses only 8, beating the next-best by up to 6.1% at 50% pruning on agentic coding.

The spread of Coding Agents is quietly reshaping the engineer's role, pushing engineers to take on management-like duties such as task assignment, progress control and delivery decisions. Agent users must shoulder a threefold responsibility: breaking down tasks, verifying results and judging when to step in; running multiple Agents in parallel does not increase output linearly and carries coordination overhead; code trustworthiness cannot rest on coverage but depends on instruction precision and the quality of the feedback loop.
Suitable for senior engineers, tech leads and practitioners of AI engineering.

An engineer's day used to begin with opening the IDE and reading code. Now, some engineers who use Coding Agents heavily start each day by checking on several AI Agents' progress: which tasks are done, which tests failed, which PRs are awaiting review, and what work needs to be reassigned.
The code is written by AI, but the engineer's job doesn't seem to have gotten any easier.

en.title: AI is getting smarter, but enterprises can barely keep it under control: Gartner's top 10 trends for 2027, with agent governance emerging as the new battleground
en.summary:
By 2031, 80% of new applications will be disposable and easily replaceable."
"By 2031, 80% of new applications will be disposable and easily replaceable."
Word count: 4,933
Reading time: about 16 minutes

Enterprise AI today faces a "high intelligence, low memory" dilemma, and the accelerating rollout of autonomous agents is forcing governance capabilities to level up. Gartner's top 10 trends for 2027 center on agent governance, with the focus shifting to controllable autonomous technologies such as context platforms, identity management and exposure remediation.

AI context platforms are becoming critical infrastructure for agents to understand business rules; agents need verifiable identities and permission boundaries rather than relying solely on model capabilities; AI coding speed has outpaced human review capacity, and accountability and pre-launch risk controls have become deployment bottlenecks.

Intended for AI platform engineers, enterprise architects, SREs and compliance leads.

"Today's AI may be the smartest digital employee in the world, but once it enters the enterprise, it has only a 3-second memory." That is how Gartner research vice president Gao Ting summed up the current state of enterprise AI.

Models are getting smarter, yet they don't understand a company's business rules, past decisions or actual operations; agents can already write code, call tools and execute tasks autonomously, but enterprises are not ready to manage these digital employees. A more immediate problem: AI generates code faster than humans can review it. Companies now have to weigh whether the generated code is usable, whether they dare ship it, and who is accountable when something goes wrong
en.reason: Gartner's 2027 ten trends frame agent governance as the next battleground, citing a “3-second memory” problem, 80% of new apps disposable by 2031, and 25% of 2028 security incidents traced to AI agent misuse.

en.title: One in two leading smartphone makers picks it: how Volcengine became the invisible backbone of AI phone assistants
en.summary:
Among China's top 10 smartphone vendors by shipment volume, one in every two is now working with Volcano Engine to upgrade the AI phone assistant experience.

Word count: 2,233 | Reading time: about 7 minutes

AI phone assistants are shifting from voice entry points to multimodal agents, which depend on coordinated audio-video interaction, multimodal understanding and on-device engineering. Volcano Engine has become the AI assistant technology foundation for 5 of China's top 10 smartphone vendors, supporting end-to-end responses within 600ms. Its full-link streaming processing and a global network of 4,000+ media nodes guarantee real-time interaction.

On-device multimodal interaction requires full-link collaborative optimization across audio and video, ASR, TTS and LLM inference

600ms is the key latency threshold for natural human-machine conversation, and Volcano Engine achieves a ≥99.5% compliance rate for 400ms

Half of China's top 10 smartphone vendors by shipment volume have adopted its AI audio-video interaction foundation

For AI device architects, intelligent voice system engineers and multimodal interaction product managers

AI phone assistants are undergoing a key shift. In the past, they were largely a "voice entry point": checking the weather, setting alarms, opening apps. Today, phone assistants are gaining stronger perception: they can hear speech and see images; answer questions and understand context; execute tasks and offer companionship in specific scenarios.
en.reason: Five of China's top 10 smartphone shippers build their AI phone assistants on Volcano Engine's audio-video stack, which targets sub-600ms end-to-end replies with a 99.5% hit rate at 400ms across 4,000+ global media nodes.

en.title: Share of developers saving dozens of hours a week with AI drops from 68% to 26% in a year
en.summary:
According to Atlassian's 2026 State of Developer Experience report, the share of developers saving more than ten hours a week through AI has dropped from 68% to 26% over the past year. Meanwhile, adoption is nearing universal coverage: 95% of developers and 96% of engineering leaders say their organizations are actively using AI in engineering work.

Developer AI usage is now near-universal, yet the share saving more than 10 hours a week has plunged 60%, driven mainly by a shift into AI management overhead rather than a lack of tools.

AI has not reduced overall work friction, only changed its shape; a high proportion of developers say AI improves delivery speed and output per unit of time; all conclusions rest on subjective self-reporting, not systematic telemetry data.

Intended for engineering productivity engineers, engineering managers, and DevEx practitioners.
en.reason: Atlassian's 2026 State of Developer Experience report shows the share of developers saving over 10 hours a week with AI fell from 68% to 26% even as 95% report organizational AI use, and it examines how AI management overhead, not tool scarcity, now shapes engineering friction.

Enterprise AI today faces a "high intelligence, low memory" dilemma, and the accelerating rollout of autonomous agents is forcing governance capabilities to level up. Gartner's top 10 trends for 2027 center on agent governance, with the focus shifting to controllable autonomous technologies such as context platforms, identity management and exposure remediation.

AI context platforms are becoming critical infrastructure for agents to understand business rules; agents need verifiable identities and permission boundaries rather than relying solely on model capabilities; AI coding speed has outpaced human review capacity, and accountability and pre-launch risk controls have become deployment bottlenecks.

Intended for AI platform engineers, enterprise architects, SREs and compliance leads.

"Today's AI may be the smartest digital employee in the world, but once it enters the enterprise, it has only a 3-second memory." That is how Gartner research vice president Gao Ting summed up the current state of enterprise AI.

Models are getting smarter, yet they don't understand a company's business rules, past decisions or actual operations; agents can already write code, call tools and execute tasks autonomously, but enterprises are not ready to manage these digital employees. A more immediate problem: AI generates code faster than humans can review it. Companies now have to weigh whether the generated code is usable, whether they dare ship it, and who is accountable when something goes wrong

OpenAI has changed Altman’s life—and unleashed a wave sweeping across the entire tech industry.

Meanwhile, adoption is nearing universal coverage: 95% of developers and 96% of engineering leaders say their organizations are actively using AI in engineering work.

Developer AI usage is now near-universal, yet the share saving more than 10 hours a week has plunged 60%, driven mainly by a shift into AI management overhead rather than a lack of tools.

AI has not reduced overall work friction, only changed its shape; a high proportion of developers say AI improves delivery speed and output per unit of time; all conclusions rest on subjective self-reporting, not systematic telemetry data.

Intended for engineering productivity engineers, engineering managers, and DevEx practitioners.
en.reason: Atlassian's 2026 State of Developer Experience report shows the share of developers saving over 10 hours a week with AI fell from 68% to 26% even as 95% report organizational AI use, and it examines how AI management overhead, not tool scarcity, now shapes engineering friction.
